correctness.rationale: Using the exact published half-line absorption quadrature, all derivatives are justified by dominated convergence. On (0,1) both derivative components are positive; on [1,sqrt(3)] both second derivatives are strictly negative. On [sqrt(3),2], a uniform lower bound on -B-prime strictly exceeds the positive part of C_m-prime. For eta>=2, an exact arctangent expression and its strictly positive comparison function prove C_2-prime<0, and a one-sign-change weight comparison proves C_m-prime<0 for every initial site at least two. Thus the unique derivative zero in (1,sqrt(3)) is the global maximum. The reciprocal identity follows by direct algebra. Beta-moment expansions give the inverse-cubic and sixth-order distance asymptotic constants. The verification file independently checks quadratures, stationarity, finite-time propagators, and large-m leading terms; none of its finite runs is used as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The exact absorption integral and remote-site reciprocal duality are explicitly prior in Riberi (arXiv:2605.08056). The new quantified claim is a global all-positive-coupling unique finite-distance optimum on the strong-loss side, exact strict reciprocal defect at every finite starting distance, and two-term optimal-shift/sixth-order gain laws. The directly matching source and relevant absorbing-walk models were compared by statements and implications, not titles; the inspected material does not supply the derivative-sign comparison or the asymptotic constants. Semantic published-record queries and accessible earlier claims showed no same statement. This is a best-knowledge originality assessment, not a guarantee of literature-wide priority.

value.rationale: Absorption efficiency is an intrinsic observable for boundary-sink transport. A sharp single optimum for every distance resolves the previously qualitative strong-loss versus weak-loss crossover and disproves the notion that critical coupling critical loss ratio one is exactly optimal at finite distance. The exact inverse-cubic shift, sixth-order improvement and strict reciprocal asymmetry quantify how boundary preparation geometry affects sink tuning; they are not arbitrary parameter instances. This motivates finite-distance transport design even though the gain becomes small for large m.
